Issued at 323 PM CDT Sun Aug 2 2026

Currently Through Tonight...

Overall been a nice end to the weekend across the area...dry  
conditions continue, with satellite imagery showing no shortage
of sunshine...though still seeing some hazy skies due to 
wildfire smoke streaming in from the north. A well-amplified 
upper level pattern remains in place across the CONUS this 
afternoon...with upper air and satellite data showing northerly 
flow across the forecast area. The Central Plains is sitting 
between a ridge axis extending from the Desert SW northeastward 
toward MN...becoming more dampened/tilted further east thanks to
a low pressure system moving through central Canada...and a 
trough axis extending from eastern Canada south to the Gulf 
Coast region. At the surface, high pressure continues to 
gradually shift off to the east...but is keeping winds light 
across easterly portions of the area. To the west and northwest,
a trough axis and frontal boundary are becoming better 
organized across the High Plains into the western 
Dakotas...bringing more solidly southerly winds to central and 
western areas, with occasional gusts near 20 MPH. No big 
surprises as far as temperatures go...forecast of mid-upper 80s 
east to low-mid 90s west remains on track.

Quiet conditions continue on into this evening and overnight.
Due to the continued deepening of the sfc low/boundaries off 
to our WNW, not expecting a drop off in winds 
tonight...remaining southerly around 10-15 MPH. Lows look to 
drop into the mid 60s for much of the area.

Early to Mid-Week...

Getting into the start of the new work week...overall there
hasn't been any significant changes to the forecast. During 
the daytime hours on Monday...models remain in good agreement 
showing an upper level disturbance working its way along the 
US/Can border into the Nrn Rockies/High Plains...the forecast 
for our area remains dry through 00Z. This system will be 
driving a surface cold front south with time...and models are 
still in decent agreement with the timing...showing at 00Z the 
placement of this front runs roughly from far SWrn NE north 
through the Sandhills and into central SD. Ahead of this front 
during the daytime hours...expecting gusty southerly winds and a
bump up in temperatures. Sustained speeds around 20-25 MPH and 
gusts around 30-35 MPH are not out of the question...with highs 
around 90 expected in the east, around 100 in the WSW. During 
the mid-late afternoon hours...the RH/wind combo hits near-
critical levels across far WSW portions of the area...but with 
fuels unfavorable for rapid fire growth, no formal headlines 
were considered...just something to be aware of. 

Main question for the evening and overnight hours Monday lies
with thunderstorm chances...still plenty of uncertainties with
the overall coverage/impact. Models showing at least scattered 
activity firing along that surface boundary to work its way into
WNW portions of the forecast area...aided by convergence along 
an increasing SSWrly low-level jet. With time, most models are 
keeping coverage of activity generally scattered in nature with 
its eastward shift...likely hindered by the fact that the better
upper level forcing is better focused to our north and that 
mid-level/temps is another element storms would have to 
overcome. As a result, the higher precip chances in the evening 
(40-60 percent) are focused across far WNW portions of the 
area...then spread east but drop into the 20-30 percent range 
overnight. 

As we get into Tuesday and Wednesday...models are in good
agreement showing that the upper level pattern has 
transitioned to more zonal in nature having further dampened the
main ridging. Chances for showers and thunderstorms continue 
both days...as additional waves of upper level shortwave energy 
push through the region. Still plenty of uncertainties with the 
details...as timing/location of chances will be greatly 
influenced by activity that happens the previous 
evening/overnight...and how that impacts the ultimate placement 
of the main surface cold front or any other lingering 
boundaries. The most uncertainty with those details lies with 
Tuesday/Tuesday night...as what happens then may provide enough 
of a reinforcing push to focus better chances further south for 
Wednesday afternoon/overnight. With the increased cloud 
cover/precipitation potential...highs for Tue-Wed cool 
some...with Tuesday currently in the mid-70s to mid-80s, 
Wednesday in the mid-70s to lower-80s.

At this point, none of the days Monday-Wednesday are included in
the SPC severe weather outlooks...though Monday/Day 2 is 
pretty close right along our NWrn edge. As mentioned above,
